utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. If there are no procedural matters, the witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness's microphones be turned on, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Welcome back to the courtroom. I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies. Mr. Tolimir is continuing his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to greet everyone present. May there be peace in this house and may these proceedings of today and in general be concluded according to God's will and not my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I would like to greet Mr. Milovanovic and I wish him a pleasant stay in the courtroom with us. Thank you. General, yesterday, for the most part, we discussed the cessation of hostilities and parts of activities related to it. We'll have a look at a number of documents, including some OTP documents. In order to conclude the topic, please tell us this. Did we, in the Main Staff, mainly receive requests on the passage of humanitarian convoys so that we could provide appropriate security at check-points for their passage? And did we have the right to stop and check the contents of such convoys along the route?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to an initial agreement that was reached in the first half of 1992, it was agreed between the UNPROFOR BiH command and the Main Staff that humanitarian aid convoys can traverse RS territory to finally reach Muslim or Croat-held territory. However, as far as I was concerned, they had to have been announced at least 24-hours in advance. That announcement should also contain the route, the proposed route of the convoy, the contents, those in charge of the convoy, and it was our obligation, just before they left the RS and entered the Muslim-Croat coalition territory, to carry out a check. At first, some tests runs were performed means that those in charge of the check-point could decide whether each and every vehicle would be inspected or whether that could be done at random. He may well have chosen a single vehicle in the whole convoy. It all functioned properly until sometime in the middle of the war. Actually, it functioned until the safety areas or the enclaves were established. Later on, we began seeing that some vehicles were transporting unannounced goods or those goods that were not permitted. We increased our checks, and we always cautioned UNPROFOR about what was going on. So sometime in mid-1994 when the enclaves were in full operation, our inspections were very strict. In addition to those inspections, if there were any aircraft involved, they were always told to land somewhere near Sokolac, if their final destination was one of the enclaves. Sometimes convoys were even returned if we discovered ammunition, weapons, or impermissible goods. Therefore, General, there was agreement in place on the passage of convoys until UNPROFOR, whose only obligation was to escort those convoys, began making mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I believe everyone understood what you just said. I have just a short follow-up question. Were humanitarian aid convoys approved by the coordination body of the RS and did the VRS approve and check only UNPROFOR convoys? This is to be able to note the difference between humanitarian aid convoys and UNPROFOR convoys.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, I'm not quite familiar who each convoy belonged to. What I know is that I was asked to cease all combat activity if it was along the route of humanitarian convoys. Humanitarian aid convoys were UNHCR convoys but they were escorted by UNPROFOR. As for UNPROFOR convoys, which were there to supply things for their own troops, that's a different matter. They could transport such goods as ammunition, if needed by their troops. However, we had problems there too. Once the safety area of Gorazde was established --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But let's deal with the convoys first.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were two different convoys. Humanitarian aid convoys and UNPROFOR convoys aimed at UNPROFOR troops within the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at P689, please. It should be page 726. It's a decision on the formation of a state committee for cooperation with international organisations, including international humanitarian organisations. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You can see the Official Gazette in which the decision was published. Let's have a look at the next page in the Serbian, as well as in English. Here it says decision on the formation of state committee for cooperation with the UN and international organisations. I wanted to read out Article 1. "Hereby a state committee is formed with cooperation with United Nations and international humanitarian organisations. The president -- or the representative -- no. The president of the republic appoints the president, deputy president and members of the committee by special decree. Article 2: "The committee is hereby formed with the aim of improving cooperation with the United Nations ..." And in Article 5, we see who the members of the committee were. Actually the working bodies of the committee. Let's look at the next page to see those. Thank you. Can you please move the text to the left. That was it. It is on the next page in English, towards the bottom of the page it says: "Decision on the appointment of representatives. President and members of the state committee for cooperation with the UN and international humanitarian organisations." Could we please go to the next page in English. It says here that "Professor Nikola Koljevic, deputy president of Republika Srpska is hereby appointed president of the state committee for cooperation with the UN and international humanitarian organisations. "Maxim Stanisic is hereby appointed deputy president of the state committee for cooperation with the UN and international humanitarian organisations." What follows are the nine members of the committee. In number 7 there seems to be a military man, Colonel Milos Djurdjic. You mentioned him yesterday. He acted as coordinator?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir. You were reading very fast again, and a specific part of your reading was not recorded. You see it on page 5, line 10. You only see the name of Maxim Stanisic, but not his function because you were too fast. Slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will repeat. "Maxim Stanisic is hereby appointed deputy president of the state committee for cooperation with the UN and international humanitarian organisations." In Article 2 we see the members of the committee. There are nine in total, including a military officer of the Main Staff in number -- under number 7. It is Colonel Milos Djurdjic, coordinator for the committee's relations with the Ministry of Defence and the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. He was discussed here yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you recall that he was a member of the committee in charge of relations with military structures?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. He was a member of the committee, and as of the moment the committee was formed, the job of the Main Staff and myself was made much easier. I no longer had to think whether I should let through a convoy. I simply knew that I had to cease all combat activities if they were en route of a particular convoy. Therefore, it wasn't up to the Main Staff to decide anymore whether the convoy would be let through or not. It was actually the task of the Main Staff to let it through and to carry out checks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we next have 65 ter 3322 in e-court. Thank you. While we're waiting for it, I will say for the record that it is a Main Staff document from the sector of intelligence and security of the 12th of February, 1995. It is signed by assistant commander, Major-General Zdravko Tolimir. I will quote the first paragraph only. "UNPROFOR representatives, through the work of regional joint commissions, keep putting forth the issue of increased freedom of movement of UNPROFOR across front lines with the aim of getting authorisation to cross the front line, move in the territory of the RS on the lower regional levels while not having to notify the Main Staff of the VRS of all movements and not having to wait for authorisation by the Main Staff of the VRS before doing so. "This is how UNPROFOR representatives wish to avoid complying with the obligation they undertook when they signed the obligations set out in the agreement on the principles of freedom of movement signed on 31 January 1995 by the Main Staff of the VRS, Major-General Zdravko Tolimir, and the UNPROFOR command for the former BiH, General Briquemont. We hereby forward the entire text of the agreement." I won't go into the rest of the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please tell us this. Do you know that we demanded that the agreement be implemented in full. It was the agreement imposed, so to say, by UNPROFOR, and UNPROFOR was a signatory to it, together with thee VRS, concerning their freedom of movement.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I would like to ask for page 2 to be shown on the screen for the General where we can see the items of the agreement. And after that, also to show page 3. And on page 3, let us read the last paragraph. I'm quoting: "These freedom of movement principles refer only to convoys and single UNPROFOR vehicles and not to convoys of international humanitarian organisations. Regarding convoys of international humanitarian organisations, implement the procedure and checks agreed upon so far. Assistant Commander, Major-General such and such." Is this a reflection of what you told us a moment ago, namely, that your work became easier after the establishment of the state committee? Or let me reformulate my question. Or maybe you can answer already? Maybe it is not necessary for me to reformulate my question.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's the same topic we discussed a moment ago. But there's something that I would like to add. Let me go back to the convoys of supplies for UNPROFOR. In April 1994, there was a certain conflict between myself and General Van Baal who was Chief of Staff for the BH UNPROFOR. He was asking for a unit, I think it was a Ukrainian contingent in Gorazde, he was asking for them to be supplied with ammunition, and I asked him whether there were any combat activities in Gorazde during the previous week. He said no. And I then asked him, But didn't you already resupply the same unit just a week before that? And he didn't respond to that. And they gave up on this idea. And our conclusion was that they are using their convoys to bring ammunition into enclaves and everybody knew that the 81st Muslim Division was established within the 3 kilometre diameter there in the enclave, with 6.500 troops and there -- no one shouldn't have been there armed and the problems between us and UNPROFOR were related to supplies of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I would like to ask for this document that's in e-court, 03322, that's the 65 ter number of the Prosecutor, I would like to tender it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 3322 shall be assigned exhibit number D254. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yesterday there was some discussion about cessation of hostilities. We showed two documents from the two meetings. The first meeting and the second meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 05838, please, if we can have that on the screen so that we can see that these meetings were held regularly, every week. Once we will have the document on the screen - there it is - and it's a Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska document, dated 6th of February, 1995. And it's headed meeting of the Joint Central Commission. And in the first paragraph it is stated: "On 5 February 1995, a meeting of the Joint Central Commission was held at the Sarajevo airport chaired by the Chief of Staff of UNPROFOR's command, General Briquemont. The delegation was led by Lieutenant-General Milan Gvero, the HVO delegation by Major-General Budimir, and the Muslim delegation by Brigadier General Hadzihasanovic. The following decisions were ... adopted and signed in the meeting of the Joint Central Commission." Under number 1 we see: "To retain the principles of full freedom of movement for all the delegations to and from the location where the Central Joint Commission is meeting. And the second item says: "All decisions of the regional joint commission shall be certified by the Central Joint Commission. And the third one is that "the regional joint commission shall continue identifying the line of defence around Sarajevo as per agreement" ... And so on and so forth. So this is my question to you. The central joint military commissions, were they signing all their decisions and forwarding them to Main Staffs for verification and then further to subordinated units in accordance with the agreement on cessation of hostilities? You can, of course, present only the position of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on what I see in front of me, I can tell that you regularly informed not only the Main Staff but also the Supreme Command. And if you can show me the last page of the document, I'd be able to verify whether you regularly signed it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show the last page of the document where we can see the stamp, received stamp, after the document had been received.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that the document was sent via teletype without your actual signature, Probably with SR. I don't see that SR. But I do see the stamp, the receipt stamp, of the last teletype station which is air force command. So you informed the Supreme Command, the Main Staff, and, from here, we see also the subordinated units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document and I would like us to see the next document dated 6th of January, 65 ter number 05835. Or D225.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Document on the screen will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 5838 shall be assigned exhibit number D255. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So now, please, 65 ter 05835, or D225.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Again, a document from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska dated 7th January 1995, and it's entitled: Meeting of the Joint Central Commission and a report about it. And it is stated here: "The third meeting of the Joint Central Commission for implementing the agreement of cessation of hostilities was held at Sarajevo airport at 1200 hours on 1st January 1995. The meeting was chaired by Lieutenant-General Michael Rose and Mr. Viktor Andreev, the representatives of Republika Srpska were Professor Aleksa Buha and General Zdravko Tolimir. The Muslim side was represented by Hasan Muratovic and General Mustafa Hajrulahovic. "The following was agreed that on 8 January 1995 an exchange of liaison officers between UNPROFOR and VRS is to be conducted. And this is my question. Was General Tolimir present at this meeting, together with the representatives of the government of Republika Srpska? In other words, Minister Buha, and was Minister Buha at the time of the meeting there in place of Professor Koljevic, because he was his deputy in the committee for relations with international representatives?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Aleksa Buha was minister of foreign affairs in the RS and, of course, it is logical that he stood in for Professor Koljevic. But as I can see from this document, it is dated on the 7th of January, 1995. That was Christmas Day. I looked at the document of 2nd of January, 1995 yesterday, so this is seven days later. And in the morning, I also saw -- today in the morning I also saw a document dated 12th of February. So it seems that meetings of the Central Committee were held every five to seven days. I don't see anything contentious in relation to your presence there, so I agree that you were present, and I believe that this should be then the second meeting since the establishment of the Central Joint Commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you General. Maybe confusion can be caused by the fact that I wrote as the date the 7th and the meeting was on the 6th, but that's because I was writing my reports on the 7th. Now can you tell me whether I was summoned by the -- or was I being invited by representatives of UNPROFOR to come to the meetings although I didn't know what the topics would be, or the results? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that you regularly attended the meetings you were invited to. And I also can tell that UNPROFOR also made sure that the meetings were held regularly, and I don't see anything strange in the fact that we would be called or invited to come to the meeting without telling us what the topic would be. That was something happening all the time. They would just invite us there and when we would be there, then they would tell us what the topic was. They would never call us to just buy us drinks or anything.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document -- oh, no, I understand that it's already part of the evidence now. Can we please have 1D719 on the screen, and we'll move to the topic mentioned by General Milovanovic in his last sentence, namely, how did each side keep their promises. Thank you. This document 1D719 is a document by General Staff of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina that was at the time in Kakanj. The date is 1st of January 1995 and the title is agreement on cessation of hostilities with guidelines. General Delic sent this document to all his subordinates. Can we please see page 3 of the agreement. We'll see the text of the agreement itself, and then we'll go back to the guide-lines issued by the General. Can we scroll down so that the General would see the text of the agreement on complete cessation of hostilities. In the first item it is stated: "The following agreement on cessation of fire dated 23 December 1994, by it the sides are agreeing to complete cessation of hostilities with the start of 2000 hours of the 1st of January, 1995 along all confrontation lines. This agreement will be in effect for initially a period of four months and will be renewed under the same condition with the agreement of the parties." Item number 2. In the second line we can see mention of the Central Joint Commission that shall be established under the auspices of UNPROFOR with initial meetings to be held at the Sarajevo airport and there will also be regional joint commissions that will be established which will constantly be in session. Thank you. That was the end of my quotation and this is my question. Can we please only see before that the last page of the agreement. Here we can see the last page. It was signed by Alija Izetbegovic, Karadzic, Rasim Delic, Mladic, Akashi and Rose. One party to the conflict did not sign it and that was HVO and their representative, the representatives of the so-called Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is my question to you: Did the VRS abide by this agreement on complete cessation of hostilities that was reached on 1st of January 1995? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, General, for showing this document to me. I have been searching for it for 17 years. I've -- was involved in making -- reaching the agreement in Bihac. It was reached primarily because of Bihac under the guidance of Jimmy Carter. I didn't even know that General Dudakovic at the time acted wilfully. I believe that he was ordered to do what he was doing from his Supreme Command. I wanted just to add that he violated the agreement only 13 days after it was concluded at the time of the Orthodox New Year. This agreement involves all safe areas. It is not strange that the Croats didn't have to sign this because they were not in charge of any of the safe areas. I don't yet understand what is it that you want me to do now. Am I supposed to confirm this document because it's not in our document; it's a document by the Muslim Supreme Command, although one can take it as such, because it includes signatures of our supreme commander and the commander of the Main Staff. It's a valid, correct document, although issued by the enemy, and this document resolved all the dilemmas about my entering into Bihac or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I would like to clarify one matter. Mr. Milovanovic, on page 14, line 15, and I read it to you: "I didn't know that General acted wilfully. I believe that he was ordered to do with -- he was doing from his Supreme Command ..." I recall that you mentioned a name which was not recorded. Can you please repeat the name of this General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suggest I repeat the whole sentence because I still have it fresh in my recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought, up till now, that General Atif Dudakovic, the commander of the 5th Corps of the Muslim army was ordered to violate the cease-fire, the four-month one. However I see from this document that General Dudakovic acted wilfully, and on the 13th of January, 1995, he violated the agreement which was signed by his supreme commander, Alija Izetbegovic, and the commander of the army, Rasim Delic, who ordered him to respect the agreement. So this would be the same as if I were to violate an order of the supreme commander, Karadzic, and Commander Mladic. Dudakovic was not held responsible for that, either to his commander or the UNPROFOR command who was a guarantor of the agreement and he was not prosecuted by any judicial organs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to repeat the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the last sentence? The interpreters didn't catch it. Only the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Although there have been, so far, four reports against him for carrying out crimes against the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I just wanted some clarification. I am unable to clearly place the names that you have just mentioned to be able to appreciate whether you've actually answered the question that was asked, which was: Did the VRS abide by this agreement on complete cessation of hostilities that was reached on the 1st of January 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we see the original document with the signature in e-court. It's P1011, a document with the signatures of the signatories of this agreement. This is P1011.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see the agreement on the cessation of hostilities, which we sent to our Main Staff, which is what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 3 to see who the signatories are. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We're obliged here to provide a correction. I said that the Croats did not sign the agreement, but, actually, the Croatian representative of the HVO, Kresimir Zubak, signed it, as well as Vladimir Soljic. This was also signed by Akashi and Rose. All of those who were supposed to sign the document did actually sign it. In order to verify the document, we are now able to see all of this here on the screen. Thank you. My question is: Were all parties obliged to respect the provisions of the agreement? The Muslims, the Serbs, the Croats, and UNPROFOR? All the parties that signed it.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But there is one signature missing here, and that is the signature of the representatives of the state of Croatia, because they were a warring party to Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they already had their forces, the equivalent of 14 brigades, on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Since this is an agreement for the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and they were supposed to sign it or they should have been forced to sign it, because the agreement was signed on 23 December. And you remember yourself very well that you, or the Main Staff, on the 25th of December after Bihac transferred me to the Glamoc front because the Croat, regular Croat army, not the HVO, the regular Croat army began attacking from Livanjsko Polje towards Grahovo and Glamoc. So they were not subject to this agreement, and now I see that they did not even sign the agreement so they were not really obliged to be bound by the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. In view of everything that you have said, is it correct that UNPROFOR did not oblige them to sign the agreement, because they assumed that they would continue with their actions until they complete what they planned because the UNPROFOR could also have called the Croats and everyone. They could have invited Brussels as well, to sign the agreement. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is yes, with a criticism of UNPROFOR. UNPROFOR did not punish the Muslims when they attacked Grmec from the Bihac security area and even though they were supposed to respect this four-month cease-fire agreement they were not obliged to do that. I already said that they violated the agreement on the 13th of January, only 13 days after it was signed, and again they were not punished. When I got close to the Bihac security area, General Rose personally hit me from the air for three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us the dates when this occurred for the transcript? And if you are able to say, are you able to tell us which targets were struck at this time?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units under my command in that section of the front moved to counter-strike on the 3rd of November, 1994. In 16 days, we re-took the captured territory, some 250 square kilometres, bringing us to the edge of the river Una and dangerously close to Bihac the town, because there was no boundary to the security area. Rose warned me to stop, otherwise I would be subject to NATO air-strikes. I replied that I didn't know, there was no marked boundary of the Bihac security zone, so I was subject to strikes on the 21st of November, my birthday, then the 22nd, and the 23rd of November. The 23rd of November he stopped because in the meantime we downed six aircraft. Then he called me in the evening and he promised to send me a letter of intent when the bombing had already been finished. In any event, he tried to strike at our personnel, our troops, but the day before I got infantry close to the other infantry, so he couldn't selectively hit just the Serbs but he would have had to hit Muslims as well, which he did not dare. He sent me the letter of intent on the 24th. I was expecting a letter of intent. Actually I received an envelope on the 24th of November in the evening. It was brought by some officer, a messenger of UNPROFOR. There would say no letter in the envelope. It contained a large-scale map of Bihac with its environs, marking the boundary of the Bihac security zone for the first time. I don't know whose administration made the error, but the boundary of the security area of Bihac was signed by Boutros-Ghali on that same day when I received it on the 24th of November, 1994, while it was proclaimed a security zone a year before, in April 1993. This means that for a year and a half, the Tuzla security zone, the Bihac one, and the Sarajevo one were not delineated and that is why he was not able to punish General Dudakovic for leaving the security zone but he could punish me when I approached his imaginary security zone. The way it was marked on that map, the boundary of the security zone was actually crossing the forward end of my forces, so I had not actually entered or crossed that boundary. And this is where the -- the lines were located one month later when this cease-fire went into effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General, sir. Please, had the NATO bombing not stopped the Republika Srpska troops under your command, would the Muslims have been defeated at that time in the Cazin Krajina and would you have threatened significantly Bihac and all the other territories from where they carried out their counter-attacks? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslims had already been defeated. I'm talking about the 5th Corps; that corps was already defeated. It had withdrawn in disarray to the town of Bihac. Before pulling out, or before the withdrawal began, they collected all Muslim villages from the entire Cazin Krajina and placed them in Bihac, just like they did in the Srebrenica area and Zepa the year before. So according to estimates at that time, there were about 180.000 refugees in Bihac at that point in time. I don't know what its population was before the war. Dudakovic was pulling everybody back into the town knowing that we would not fire at the town. And it's true, we did not fire at the town with large-calibre weaponry. We did use smaller calibres in the surrounding. I was afraid that some unit would not actually enter the town. We had just reached the hospital area. So I had left a 4 kilometre buffer area between the Una river and the village of Pokoj. So that that population, if our forces did break through, because I did not have a decision by the Supreme Command to enter Bihac, if there was a breakthrough by our forces, so that the people would have a route to leave because I really afraid our forces would enter Bihac and I was afraid of possible retaliation. So I issued an order that I had forgotten about. I found it somewhere on the Internet while I was preparing for this testimony about the conduct of units in the event they entered Bihac. However, it never occurred to me to actually enter Bihac and you know very well, General, that I was a victim of the withdrawal of the Army of Republika Srpska from the strangest security area on the planet, this is Igman and Bjelasnica. For months I was trying to get that army to pull back to Igman and Bjelasnica and then it was up to me to turn them back from Igman and Bjelasnica. And, again, UNPROFOR violated the agreement and or actually permitted the Muslims to capture or retake those territories just one month later. Your question, I think, is more or less referring to where I was struck, where the strikes were. First, the Udbina airport was hit, this airport of the Serbian army of the Krajina. Then there was an attempt to strike the forward end of the Serbian forces and this could not be done because of the proximity of the Muslim forces. Then they hit the rear behind the front lines. However, there was a miracle from that area. He did not strike at my command post even though it was exposed and open to strikes. I don't know why he did not hit the personal command post. It's something that I never discussed with General Rose.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Milovanovic, I didn't interrupt you while you were answering at length but I would like to invite you as well to slow down a bit. I think some sentences are not properly recorded because of the speed of your answer and this is very difficult for the interpreters and for the court recorder. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I wanted to intervene at page 20, line 13, it says [In English]: "Dudakovic was pulling everybody back into the town." [Interpretation] I believe the witness said that he pulled all of his troops inside the town, and perhaps that should be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is up to your client, Mr. Tolimir, to clarify that. You are his advisor. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovanovic -- actually, Mr. President. Mr. Milovanovic, for the record, can you tell us whether Dudakovic pulled both his soldiers and the population inside Bihac so as to make it clear.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Dudakovic at the time was the absolute master in Bihac and its surrounding. He held in his hands both the military and civilian powers because a few days before that the minister of the interior was killed. He clashed with the rebelled soldiers of Fikret Abdic. Until the problem with Abdic and the Serbs was resolved, he was accorded absolute authority by Izetbegovic. He probably intercepted my orders not to fire at Bihac with artillery. He made use of that to move his units of his corps and the brigade to initially pull back into town for rest and later, when he had to withdraw all of his troops before my advancing forces, he withdrew his front lines to Bihac as well. At the same time, he gathered all of the population around Bihac from the Cazin Krajina into Bihac so as to have the population mix with the troops, much as they did in Srebrenica. In this way, he wanted to ensure that I could not target the soldiers without firing at civilians. Otherwise, what would have occurred would have been this fantastic construction of NATO called collateral damage because no one would acknowledge that I was trying to fire at soldiers. In other words, Dudakovic gathered both soldiers and civilians into the town itself, in order to protect his troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. In your answer, you said that NATO aviation bombed the airport at Udbina which is -- which was in the protected zone of UNPROFOR in the RSK. It was the so-called UNPA area. Is this the first occasion in the wars in the territory of the former FRY when NATO bombed an area under its own protection when Serbs were in question and, on the other hand, they never bombed UN-protected areas where the Muslims were?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, was that a question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did NATO ever bomb territories protected by the UN where there were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that, NATO had bombarded the safety area of Gorazde but not the Muslims. They targeted the Serbs approaching Gorazde. On this occasion they bombed the airport at Udbina, and it was the first occasion on which they bombed an UNPROFOR-protected area. The Vance Plan was in force in the RSK and UNPROFOR was the guarantor of it, as well as the FRY. However, when Udbina was bombed, it had far more reaching consequences. On the 20th of November, that is to say, a day before, in Zagreb, General Novakovic, Mile Novakovic Commander-in-Chief of the Army of the RSK signed agreement with the Commander-in-Chief of the Croatian army, General Bobetko, to place Udbina airport out of operation. It had been agreed that the Serb side was to implement it in the following way, by pulling out old trucks and tanks and placing them on to the air strip so as to make any sorties impossible by Serb planes. In the evening of that day General Novakovic indeed did so. He placed a number of vehicles on the runways. And the next day, on the 21st of November, they became ideal targets for NATO pilots. They destroyed the runways. I know that two people were killed in the air traffic tower, a lieutenant and an operator. There were a number of wounded, and, of course, all of the vehicles on the runways were destroyed. They were made use as targets by NATO pilots. It was NATO who targeted UNPROFOR-protected areas, and I stress that it was done by NATO, not by UNPROFOR. NATO, in that year, took over from UNPROFOR as being the only armed force of the Security Council. I heard rumours that it was not approved by the Security Council. I never tried to research that any further, but I also know that they did not have permission to bomb Yugoslavia, and yet they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovanovic. We will later on look at what Mr. Rose had to say about it in his testimony. Was there basically a coordination action between NATO and the Croatian army when the airport at Udbina was targeted? When they targeted the vehicles that were placed there under the agreement? Was this a coordinated action between the two forces, including NATO planes? And was it a mere coincidence or a planned activity?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would -- could we get some indication of the relevance of this detailed account of NATO and UNPROFOR in periods and places that I -- have no apparent connection to our case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, can you help us?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, and I'd like to thank you Mr. McCloskey. The relevance is that it speaks to the behaviour of UNPROFOR at the time of the cessation of hostilities. That is to say, their behaviour towards the Serbs who honoured the agreement and the behaviour towards the Muslims who broke the agreement. Later on, we'll get to the results of such conduct by UNPROFOR and NATO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to say, Mr. President, that this agreement on the cessation of hostilities was supposed to be in force by the initial four months and that the VRS abided by it. The General told us how his forces were bombed and whenever Muslim forces launched an attack in the latter period of the four months, they were supported in doing so. Ultimately, NATO planes took part in the bombing of war positions in Republika Srpska, including a number of bridges. A number of bridges were targeted, say, in Serbia even, which existed on places which could be simply crossed on foot. The rivers were that shallow in certain places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, every incident has a history. That's true. There are always some events preceding the relevant events, relevant to this case and to the indictment. I would like to invite you to focus on the events relevant to the indictment period, mid-1995. This would be much more helpful for your case. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We are going straight to mid-1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: Would the events in Srebrenica and Zepa have taken place which is something I'm accused of, had the truce been honoured, had it been prolonged in April? And had there been no further increase in combat activities?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's extremely vague. We need to know what he is talking about. Otherwise, the answer has no meaning. When he says the events that is he charged with, is he talking about the murders, is he talking about the other events? I mean, there's quite a bit to that. So that is, in my view, has to be more particular as to have meaning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Carry on, please, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't know what I'm supposed not to say. I was accused of contributing to the Muslim defeat in Srebrenica. As part of that indictment, I have to start with the facts which caused the Srebrenica enclave to become a source of threat for the VRS. It was supposed to have been a demilitarized zone, and instead it was a well-armed area. If I'm not allowed to pursue that line of questions I can only thank the General for his testimony and then we can move on to whatever Mr. McCloskey wishes to pursue or what you may wish to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this is a misrepresentation of what Mr. McCloskey said. And what I was saying to you, invited you to focus more on the events mid-1995. You can't draw from the record anything like that you just have said that are you not allowed to pursue that line of questions. This is some guidance and some assistance for your case, Mr. Tolimir. You should understand that. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to make it absolutely clear, I have no problem with questions to General Milovanovic about the causes or the reasons why the VRS felt it would be necessary to attack the Srebrenica enclave. In fact, as I've said over and over again, we agree with many of those reasons and understand them and they're part of our case. If that's the question, that's no problem. I don't mind the question of why is it that -- you know, the murders took place. But it just needs to be the question. We can't tell what the question is by the way he asked it. It is not the subject matter. It's just the vagueness of the question that concerns me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you have heard everything. Please carry on your questioning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have, Your Honour. But in order to get to Srebrenica, we need to see what caused Srebrenica and Zepa. Could we please look at D53. Then we can see the relevance of that document in relation to the events in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we have to make clear what you want to do with the document, 1D719. The document signed by Mr. Delic. What is your intention?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The intention is for the General to see who it was sent to. If I'm forbidden to say anything or to mention names, then can I address a single village --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Tolimir, this is really an incorrect response. I am asking what are you doing with the -- are you tendering the document you have used. Please focus on what I'm saying. That was really not correct. I want to know if you are tendering 1D719.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. I thought you were just asking me about the document I just called up and not the previous one. I apologise again. I seek to tender the previous document. And we now wanted to look at the current document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have to go back to 1D719. I would like to see the document itself and then the attachment. Perhaps not the attachment but one part of it. I would like to see the signature. Mr. Milovanovic -- no, not this part. I want to see 1D719. The signature of Mr. Delic who is supposed to have signed it. It was just on the screen before. Yes, thank you very much. Mr. Milovanovic, when did you see this document the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, here, now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, can you explain how we could authenticate this document. There is no signature. We have only the B/C/S text without any translation. The witness couldn't say anything about its content. He saw it the first time here in the courtroom. He saw the original agreement with the documents -- with the -- with the signatures. This is P1011. This is already in evidence. But this document, he can't say anything about it. Can you help us? Perhaps Mr. McCloskey can help us. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Ms. Stewart tells me that she has sent the translation recently and they may not have had time to put it into e-court. But there should be a translation of this document that's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But is there any document with a signature?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Apparently not, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the agreement, I would like to see the signature block of the agreement again. That could be or should be the next page. It is interesting to see that there is no signature at all and that two names are missing. The names of Mr. Soljic and Mr. Zubak, the representatives of the army. There is some doubt that this is really the original document. I have no idea why these names are missing. Can you help us, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. That was the reason why I showed the 1D719 and its content because the content is identical to what's in P1011, which does include signature and can confirm the authenticity of the document signed by Delic. I understand the General. Of course, he could not have seen documents drafted by the opposing side or the enemy. This is a document that drafted on 1st of January, 1995 on cessation of hostilities signed by Delic. But we can see Delic's actual signature on the other document. If that is not sufficient, well, we, of course, cannot have it admitted. There's nothing I can do about it in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we please see the letter -- the page with the name Rasim Delic again. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If it is of any help, I can tell you, Mr. President, the document on the left, the B/C/S document, was obtained by the OTP from the Republika Srpska archives in Banja Luka where we have obtained other materials. So that's where it is -- it is from. I -- I can't tell immediately by looking at it if it is a teletype. But, as you know, teletypes don't have signatures. That's where it comes from, if that is at all helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It might be a teletype. But there is no stamp, there is nothing, which is usually combined with the teletype document sent out or received by somebody. There's exactly nothing on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely. And I -- of course, we can't tell how a document might have ended up in an archive, a draft or something else. But it did come from this official government archives is, unfortunately, all I can tell you about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber will -- the Chamber will postpone a decision until we have received the translation of the document. Then we can compare the content and if it is really the same document or not. For today, we just mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D719 shall be assigned exhibit number D256, marked for identification, pending further identification. Thank you. Pending translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, not pending translation. We decide on the admission of this document after having received a translation. This is different. We didn't decide about the admission yet. We should have D53 on the screen now, please. Mr. Tolimir, now the document is on the screen. You should continue your questioning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This document was received also from the OTP. These are the documents by the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and their General Staff. Documents that were not being delivered to the VRS. We can see a document dated 17th of June, 1995 before us, General. It's called: Preparations for offensive combat operations order. It was delivered to the command of the 28th Division of KoV. I will read the first paragraph and items in the order. I quote: "Pursuant to verbal order issued by the commander of the General Staff of the BH army, army General Rasim Delic, and on the occasion of the great success achieved by units of the BH army in the wide area around Sarajevo and Gorazde ... as well as on the basis of intelligence that ... commands of the AS of the protection regiment in Han Pijesak is holding part of its units in reserve to intervene in the event of an attack by our forces from Zepa. I hereby issue the following order. "1, execute all preparations in the command of the 28th Land Army Division to execute offensive combat operations with a view to liberating the territory of BH, overextending the AS and inflicting losses on them, coordinating action with the BH army forces carrying out operations in the broader Sarajevo area. " ... plan realistic tasks," and so on and so forth. In item 3, it is stated: "The General Staff of the BH army will regulate, by an order, the commencement of offensive combat activities in the zone ... "Chief of Staff of the 2nd Corps, Brigadier Sulejman Budakovic." In other words he spend that order from the 2nd Corps command of the 28th Division which encompassed the forces from Zepa and Srebrenica. And this is my question: Can we see from this document that the BH army is carrying out active operations in Sarajevo, as is stated here, and that he is asking for all of his forces to start activities, even those in the demilitarized zones? And, please, any further comments on the document, if you have them.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, this document is not a document I'm seeing for the first time. I have seen it during the activities of the commission of the Republika Srpska government on determining facts. I have seen another document that you may also have issued by the same Chief of Staff to the Supreme Command, in relation to an attack they carried out against our Main Staff. However, you put a question to me first, and then there was a discussion, namely, the question was whether the four-month truce had any impact on what happened in Srebrenica and Zepa later on. That was my understanding at least. I'm not sure that the others present here understood you in the same way. No, the truce mediated by Carter did not influence situation in Srebrenica and Zepa but something else did. And that was failure to abide by Article 60 of the First Protocol of the Geneva Conventions, actually, Articles 58 and 60 that discussed organisation of safe areas and the rules on behaviour within such areas. One of the elements was that if one side violates the agreement, then the other side is not obliged to abide by it. The agreement on safe areas - Srebrenica was signed on 8th of May, and I think Zepa on 18th of May - was immediately violated by the party that guaranteed the agreement, namely, UNPROFOR. And the Muslim side as well. And they continued violating it until the month of July 1995, when Serb forces entered Srebrenica. In what way? First of all, UNPROFOR failed to disarm the Muslims in Srebrenica and Zepa. They incorrectly informed or reported to the Supreme Command of the VRS and the UN Security Council that Muslims in Srebrenica and Zepa were disarmed. I mentioned yesterday it was determined that 1.200 barrels of obsolete infantry and hunting weapons were handed over, that UNPROFOR received about 900 barrels of similar type of weaponry. In other words, weapons remained both in Srebrenica and Zepa. In January 1994, in the enclaves of Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde, there were functioning commands in Srebrenica of the 28th Operative Group, Eastern Bosnia, that was its name. Unit of a division strength. In Zepa, the command of the light infantry brigade, or of a light infantry brigade. And in Gorazde, command of the 81st Muslim Division. All under wings of UNPROFOR. In other words, Muslims were armed and organised, and UNPROFOR knew about it, but according to the agreement, it was not supposed to be that way. Secondly, from the safe area of Gorazde, starting in late March 1994, armed formation of Muslim whose strength was about 750 troops, which is a weak brigade or a very strong battalion level, they broke out, got through UNPROFOR deployment area, managed to get through our positions and make an incursion into Sjemec mountain area which is between Ustipraca, Visegrad, and another location. The commander was Mr. Sedic. They caused havoc; killing, raping, looting. Following that group, Lieutenant-Colonel Zivko [as interpreted] Pandurevic whose unit was in the area of Sjemec because for a period of time he was the commander of the Visegrad Brigade. So he is following Sedic and approaching Gorazde. The commander of the Herzegovina Corps reaches the conclusion that the right bank of Drina needs to be put under our control because UNPROFOR is obviously not doing it, so following this group that made an incursion against our territory out of Gorazde and then Muslims start complaining. General Rose, who had just arrived in the area, goes to Gorazde, to see for himself whether Serbs were destroying Gorazde as claimed or not. I think he managed to get in in his second attempt and realizes that the buildings destroyed in Gorazde were destroyed about two years before that, and that they were destroyed by Muslims who were driving Serbs out of Gorazde. So let us go back to the beginning of 1994. In Srebrenica, Zepa and Gorazde there is 16.500 armed Muslim troops organised in a military matter, and all this with UNPROFOR knowledge. Yesterday I mentioned Operation Parachute and ammunition that was found, ammunition 12.7-millimetres and downwards, all of that packed into flour sacks. We registered all such incidents and reported them to UNPROFOR but no action is being taken. And here is this order then. I believe this is an order issued by the Supreme Command because I can see it says at the top "Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina". And here they're ordering the 28th division, which was a successor of the operative group Eastern Bosnia, under the command of Naser Oric. He was responsible for killing for thousands of Serbs in the area of Srebrenica, wider area of Srebrenica, until we managed to suppress his forces. Now this -- Oric is doing the same as the officer from Gorazde was doing. He would go out, loot, take food, rape and pillage and kill people there and then return to Srebrenica and nobody does anything. We knew, unlike in case of Operation Storm by Croats, Tolimir, we knew that the Muslims are preparing an offensive. It was scheduled to start on the 16th of June, 1995. It lasted for a period of nine days and it failed. As part of that offensive, and we can see this in the document before us, the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina orders the 28th Division to tie up the forces in the area so that the Main Staff could not use them and send them to help the defence of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm very, sorry, Mr. Milovanovic, your answer took, up to now, nearly -- more than ten minutes. I was not expecting such a length of your answer. We are running out of time. We must have our first break now. Otherwise, the tape will be -- has -- the tapes have to be rewound. I'm very sorry for interrupting you during your answer, but I'm sure you will be able to say, after the break, what you have to say. Thank you very much. We must adjourn, and we will resume ten minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before the break, we heard a very lengthy answer by Mr. Milovanovic. I would like to raise one matter. There's no doubt that there is was a war in the State of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and there's no doubt that many crimes were committed by several parties and people. I think, Mr. Tolimir, you should realize that you are charged in this Tribunal and in this case with several crimes, and you should ask questions about the background, about this -- these charges, about the indictment against you. And I would like to ask the witness to focus on this indication and to listen carefully to the questions put to you and to answer these questions and not to give lengthy explanation of all details of specific periods of the war. We should all do our best to use the court time properly and not to waste time. We have to make sure that this trial is fair but also expeditious. Please carry on and put the next question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, General, since you've seen the order I asked you about, let me repeat me question. What were the consequences of this order, in relation to events in Srebrenica and Zepa? Is there any link between them? Was this maybe a cause of the events that I'm being charged with here?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order and orders such as this one were directly linked with what happened in, first, Srebrenica and then Zepa. The units of the 28th Division were, even prior to receiving this order, had attacked a village of Visica, a Serbian village, that is in the vicinity of Srebrenica on their way to our Main Staff. I think that was the fourth Muslim attack against the Main Staff. On three occasions, I was in charge of the defence. All of the four attacks came from Srebrenica and Zepa. First one was on the 7th of August, 1992. The forces started -- set off from Zepa. The second one was in the period between 11 and 16th of December, 1992. The forces set out from Srebrenica. The third one was a minor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sir, I have to interrupt you. Now are you talking about 1992. The document is from the 17th of June, 1995. And the question was: What were the consequences of this order? Please focus on this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Direct consequences of this order was an attack against a command post of the Main Staff. In repelling that attack, the units, first, of the Main Staff, and, then, later on of the Drina Corps, who were chasing away the Muslim army after their attack against the Main Staff in Visica, following them, approached Srebrenica. An army that has been attacked is entitled to follow and destroy the attacking forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You were interrupted sometime ago while you were talking about the Sarajevo offensive that lasted for nine days and about the events in Srebrenica where a bloodshed occurred and in which Naser Oric participated. My question is the following: The events in Sarajevo and the events from 1993 in Srebrenica, did they have any consequences on the events that took place later on, in 1995, in July and 1995, and for which I am charged? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this is a very vague question, very vague. Did events in Sarajevo and events from 1993 in Srebrenica have any consequence on the events that took place later on. What do you mean by that? Please put a specific question. Otherwise we will get into history and get very lengthy answers. This is not helpful for your case. Please put a specific question to the witness which can be answered in brief.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, was the commander of the Main Staff of the BH army making combat disposition of their forces in order to spread out our forces during the main operation of unblocking the siege of Sarajevo at the time of this nine-day offensive you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because the Supreme Commander of the Muslim forces used the safe areas as areas from which surprise operations were carried out against VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Was the VRS forced to repel such attacks coming from enclaves towards the areas outside of the enclaves and the Main Staff? Was that a legitimate military action?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the Muslim forces began their incursions into RS territory from Srebrenica, the VRS was relieved of its obligation to honour Article 60 of the First Protocol to the Geneva Conventions and was free to respond. What I said a moment ago, we were then entitled to pursue the enemy to its complete elimination and until it ceases to be a threat to us, which is as long as they were in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have a look at P193, page 9, to see what General Smith had to say about that period. He was the UNPROFOR commander in Bosnia at the time, and had data on their weapons. And it was immediately prior to their total annihilation in Srebrenica and Zepa. This is his statement of 14th August 1996 and he repeated this in his testimony. Could we look at the next page, paragraph 5, it says as follows: "The eastern enclaves were" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Tolimir, could you please give a reference to the English version of it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. As I don't speak English, my legal assistant will tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Your legal assistant should have helped you before our hearing. Find it immediately and not to waste time. And note that this document is not listed in your list of documents to be used during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It isn't?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't find it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I omitted to tell him that I would refer to this document; in all other respects he is very diligent. By your leave, I wanted to quote from the second line of the fifth paragraph, on page 10. In the English version. Actually, it's page 8. It begins with the words: "The eastern enclaves ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... This is not on the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 8 in the English please. Can we have it on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, please assist your client so that we can find the respective page. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies, Mr. President. It is the next page in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The third.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone is off, Mr. Tolimir. Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. "The eastern enclaves were too strong and the Bosnian army within them constituted a clear threat, particularly as the Bosnian Serb army felt they were likely to face attacks on multiple fronts. In the enclaves, the UN were being used as shield by the Bosnians and a hostage by the Serb."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is my question: Did the UNPROFOR command, too, know that there were strong forces in the enclaves that were armed to their teeth?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they knew that throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at page 11 of the statement in the Serbian. In the English language, it is page 12. It is the first paragraph on the Serbian page, beginning at the words: "During April ..." It is the second paragraph in the English version. Mr. Smith says as follows: "During April the situation in Bosnia worsened. The enclaves were so logistically pressed that I drew up a new plan of supplying them by helicopter. This was -- meant provoking the VRS to attack the helicopter and then to bomb them." Actually another sentence: "This plan was put before the UN forces command in Zagreb and New York but was seen as too risky and confrontational." My question is this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the record, it is not page 12 in English but page 10, which is now on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are correct, Mr. President. It is the last paragraph on page 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... not the last paragraph. Sorry. We have it now and we see it in the middle of the page. Now your question please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Given that I don't speak the language, I won't try to pin-point any portions anymore in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: General, would it have been more logical for General Smith to ask for approval to demilitarise the zones instead of looking for an excuse to bomb the VRS, which would have produced better results, in terms of reducing any further combat activities and minimizing any further escalation of the war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was waiting for the transcript, Your Honour. One can foresee my answer because it is only logical. Rupert Smith was new. I could see that he had previously established that the enclaves had not been disarmed, and he should have done what his predecessors failed to do. The predecessors being Morillon and Briquemont. Instead of finding ways to supply the enclave, he was supposed to perform the job as ordered to UNPROFOR by the Security Council. My response is simply that by acting this way, Smith simply deepened the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Given the different treatment by NATO and UNPROFOR toward -- to the two opposing sides, was any activity undertaken by the Muslims tolerated by UNPROFOR and NATO and even supported, and any activity on the part of the VRS was suppressed and punished by air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only speak to the parts of the front that I was at, and there, it was true. Any mistake by Muslims was forgiven, whereas, any mistake made by the Serbs, punished. The examples are the ones I used already, Mount Igman and Bjelasnica. When my units were withdrawing at a check-point in the presence of UNPROFOR, Muslims killed 37 unarmed soldiers of mine and wounded another 34. I sent a letter of protest with a threat to General Rose. He did not react to it, but he did not fail to mention it later on in his memoirs and he said I was right, but he also failed to explain what it was that he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to thank my legal assistant. It seems that it was not recorded that they were killed in the presence of UNPROFOR. Could you please repeat that part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, the transcript has finished. We are waiting for your answer. Mr. Tolimir asked to you repeat a specific part which is supposed not to have been translated and recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies. I was trying to figure out which of the 13 UNPROFOR checkpoints it was. I think it was the Tresnjevo Brdo checkpoint. It was in the presence of UNPROFOR. From that hill they were supposed to prevent the Muslims from capturing Mount Igman and Bjelasnica. Our forces were in withdrawal. The UNPROFOR came to take up their duties and a group of Muslim soldiers came, killing 37 and wounding 34 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. If, throughout the war, UNPROFOR treated the VRS and the Muslims differently, and if the VRS was prevented from defending its territory and people, could that have had consequences for the overall conduct of the Muslim army vis-a-vis their obligations under the agreement on the cessation of hostilities?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, without fail.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You participated in the end-game operations, and you can testify to it. Can you tell us whether, at that time, members of UNPROFOR and NATO also displayed bias, tolerating Muslim activities and punishing the Serbs for any legitimate resistance operation? Was that so, and did that situation culminate on the 13th of August, when VRS units, as well as all of its communications and command centres, were attacked?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the theatre where I was defending our part of the country from Operation Storm, which means to the west, UNPROFOR and the European Rapid Intervention Corps, commanded by General Soubirou, a French general, offered fire support to the Croats, the regular Croat army. The Muslims also supported the Croats by manoeuvres and fire support --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Milovanovic, may I interrupt you. You were asked about the 13th of August, and we were dealing with the war and crimes in -- committed in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and not the war related to Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it may be my fault for not displaying a document, in which case I will. It's a document about the bombing of VRS positions towards the end of the war. I believe I am entitled to address that issue because it may be relevant to prove bias on the part of NATO and UNPROFOR when treating the Serbs and Muslims and Croats. Could we please have 1D776.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see that this is a document from the Main Staff of the VRS dated the 30th of August, 1995. The title is: NATO aviation strikes in the area of responsibility of the corps specified, information. I quote: "Early in the morning, on 30th of August, 1995, NATO forces carried out two extensive air-strikes on targets chosen beforehand. The first strike took place between 1.40 and 2.40 hours with 40 planes, of which 30 were assault aeroplanes. The combat lasted for ten minutes between 1.55 and 2.05 hours. The second comprehensive attack included 30 planes of which 20 were assault jets, between 3.40 and 4.45. The combat itself lasted for ten minutes, between 4.00 and 4.10." Let's look at the beginning of the second paragraph: "During these two comprehensive air-strikes, the enemy attacked the general region of the command of the Main Staff without any consequences. They also attacked the radar positions at Jahorina, Stolice, Krug, as well as the post and telegraph relay station at Straziste, Cajnice, Trebevic. The former radio relay station at Zlovrh, as well as the self-propelled rocket battery in the general area of Sokolac. At 3.20 they also attacked the communications facility Kraljica at Mount Ozren. The enemy inflicted losses in terms of personnel and caused damage to the facilities. Obviously the goal of enemy action was to damage and destroy command and communications centres in order to eliminate the chain of command and control at strategic and operational levels." By virtue of this bombing in August, did the NATO Alliance, attacking the RS throughout its territory, side with the Croat-Muslim Federation, assisting the attack from Croatia by destroying communications and command centres throughout RS territory?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now have 1D774 on the screen, and I would also like to tender the previous document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D776 shall be assigned exhibit number D257, marked for identification, pending translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thanks to the e-court, we have the document before us. This is a document issued by the Main Staff of the VRS, dated 21st of September, 1995. And what is discussed in this document are the consequences and the resolution of the consequences of the air-strikes. The commander is here issuing an order regarding the consequences of the air-strike in the barracks in Han Pijesak, and I will just read the first item. "The commander of the Han Pijesak barracks will, together with the commander of the 67th Communications Regiment, engage all available troops and start with the repairing and making the facilities functional again in accordance with the plan made by the commander of the Han Pijesak barracks." In the introduction, we can read the following: "After the NATO Alliance air-strikes against Han Pijesak barracks, a damage was caused which made those facilities completely ineffective." Can we please see the last page so that we can see the signature in the document, on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: As can you see, this is an order issued by General Mladic. Did you also know about the air-strikes against the barracks in Han Pijesak, and did you see their activities and the consequences of those activities on the facilities in Han Pijesak and facilities around the Main Staff? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear about the operations, partly from this order that I also received. I did not have any troops or barracks that were attacked by NATO, except those that had to do with communication hubs, and I also felt the fire that was used by the Euro Corps and I don't know why was I not allowed to talk about it. But the Euro Corps was the fifth military power that appeared in the theatre of war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It represented an attempt by the European Community to create a military organisation of its own, similar to the NATO Alliance, and they used Bosnia as their trial theatre of war.
